projects.title: Portfolio & Blog
projects.blurb: React, Express and MongoDB with JWT auth, an admin dashboard and a comment system. Front and back deployed separately.
projects.problem: I had projects scattered across GitHub and notes scattered across Notion. I wanted one place where a recruiter could read a paragraph about me, click into a project, and see that I can finish things.
built: Six REST resource groups (users, projects, posts, comments, messages, matches) behind a single error handler.
JWT auth with a protect middleware and author-only checks on every write route.
An admin area with full CRUD for projects and posts, optimistic UI and a confirm step on delete.
A public debate page that works logged-out and saves match history when logged in.
projects.learned: Auth is not a feature you add at the end. The first version had every route open, and retrofitting ownership checks touched almost every controller.
projects.statusNote: Deployed and testable end to end: register, log in, comment, send the contact form, then read it in the admin inbox. 27 endpoints, 68 automated assertions, all green.

projects.title: Debate Simulator
projects.blurb: 100 debate topics, three AI opponents and a five-axis scorer — all inside one dependency-free HTML file.
projects.problem: I wanted to practise arguing in English but every 'AI chat' tool felt like talking to a very polite wall — it agreed with whatever I said. I needed something that pushed back, immediately, with no server and no signup.
built: A 100-topic library, each with pro/con keyword groups and four sample arguments so the bot never runs out of things to say.
A five-axis scorer: logic, relevance, length, rebuttal, examples. Pure slogans score zero, bad advice scores negative.
The bot quotes the exact words you just used before disagreeing — no invented claims about your position.
Speech input via Web Speech API, with a clear fallback message when the browser does not support it.
projects.learned: Shipping everything in one file forced me to be honest about what actually earns points. Half of the scoring rules came from reading my own bad arguments back.
projects.statusNote: Runs: the single-file build is playable in the browser and the scoring behaves as described. Not a product — no accounts, no server, progress stays in localStorage.

projects.title: Campus Marketplace
projects.blurb: A small marketplace for students: post, search, message, browse by faculty, with images going straight to cloud storage.
projects.problem: Second-hand trading at my school happened in WeChat groups: unsearchable, reposted hourly, and impossible to browse by anything except scrolling.
built: Listing model with faculty, condition and price, plus compound indexes for the search endpoint.
Direct-to-Cloudinary upload using a signed request, so the API never proxies image bytes.
In-app messaging with a simple unread counter instead of exposing phone numbers.
Moderation queue: reported listings are hidden until a moderator approves them.
projects.learned: Search quality is mostly schema design. Once faculty and condition were indexed properly, the 'search is slow' complaints disappeared without touching the query.
projects.statusNote: Design concept only. The data model and upload flow are thought through; there is no running build, so read the list below as scope rather than finished features.

projects.title: Course Scheduler
projects.blurb: Drag-and-drop weekly timetable that detects time clashes before you commit to them.
projects.problem: Course registration gives you a list of sections, not a week. I kept signing up for things that overlapped and finding out two days later.
built: A 5×10 grid with drag-and-drop sections and keyboard fallback for accessibility.
Conflict detection that highlights the exact overlapping pair instead of a generic error.
Local persistence plus export to a calendar file.
A condensed mobile view: one day per column, sections stacked.
projects.learned: Drag and drop is 20% dragging and 80% edge cases — dropping outside the grid, dropping onto yourself, and undoing a drop nobody asked for.
projects.statusNote: Concept only — the grid, the conflict rules and the keyboard fallback are specified, nothing is implemented yet.

projects.title: Screen Time Dashboard
projects.blurb: A year of my own app usage turned into a readable dashboard — because the built-in one told me nothing.
projects.problem: The system screen-time report shows one number per day. I wanted to know which apps were eating the time, and whether the pattern changed on weekends.
built: CSV ingestion with a column mapper, so a different export does not break the chart.
Stacked area chart by app category, with a weekend/weekday split.
Brushable timeline that filters every other chart on the page.
An honest note about missing days instead of interpolating them.
projects.learned: Most of the work was cleaning, not charting. And showing a gap is more truthful than a smooth line that never happened.
projects.statusNote: Concept only. The chart ideas exist as sketches; no ingest pipeline or chart has been written.

projects.title: Habit CLI
projects.blurb: A terminal habit tracker that stores everything in one readable JSON file you can edit by hand.
projects.problem: Every habit app wants an account. I wanted something that works over SSH on the school server and survives a sync conflict.
built: Four commands: add, check, streak, export. No config file required.
Streak calculation that understands 'skip days' so a planned rest does not break a run.
Atomic writes to a plain JSON file — safe to edit while the tool is not running.
Human-readable diff on every write, so you can see what changed.
projects.learned: A CLI is a UI too. The help text took longer than the storage layer, and it is what people actually judge the tool by.
projects.statusNote: Concept only — commands and file format are specified, there is no working binary.

posts.title: From design to a URL someone else can open
posts.excerpt: The capstone worked on my machine in week one and took three more weeks to become a link a stranger could open. Here is what actually broke: four hosting platforms, one rewritten response header, and a PATCH request that never reached my code.

body.text: The brief was two pieces: a REST API with Node and Express over MongoDB Atlas, and a React single-page app that consumes it. The interesting part was never the CRUD. It was the gap between "npm start works" and "open this URL on your phone". That gap ate more time than the API did.
What I designed first

Six collections: users, projects, skills, posts, comments, messages. Every write route sits behind a JWT, and every write route also checks ownership — the user id comes from the token, never from the request body, so a forged body field is simply ignored. The admin dashboard reads the same collections the public pages read, which means a bug shows up in two places instead of hiding in a panel nobody opens.

One decision paid for itself repeatedly: a single error handler. A malformed ObjectId returns 404 instead of a 500 with a Mongoose stack trace, and every error comes back as the same { success, message, errors } shape, so the client has exactly one branch to write.
Platform one through four

Render wanted card verification I could not complete. Railway had suspended new sign-ups after a breach. My Vercel account was restricted with no appeal path. A container host did start the app — the logs were clean — but only served 404s from its edge, and its free URL expired after sixty minutes.

I stopped optimising for "which platform is best" and started optimising for "which platform will still answer on the day I have to demo this". That turned out to be Alibaba Cloud Function Compute for the API plus GitHub Pages for the static build. Not the fashionable answer, but it produced two URLs that a teacher can open without installing anything.
Bug one: the gateway rewrites your headers

On the function host's default domain, every response is served with Content-Disposition: attachment. Not my code — the gateway adds it after my handler returns. Browser navigation therefore downloads a JSON file instead of rendering it, which looks exactly like a broken deployment to anyone evaluating the link.

fetch() and XHR ignore that header, so the app was never actually broken. But "it works if you use the right tool" is a bad answer for a graded submission. I moved the front end to GitHub Pages — a different origin, so nothing inherits the header — and left the API where it was. The fix was architectural, not a one-line patch.
Bug two: PATCH never reached Express

The admin inbox has a "mark as read" button. It returned 403 in production and 200 locally. The request was not being rejected by my auth middleware — it was rejected by the HTTP trigger, before Express saw it. The platform's gateway does not allow the PATCH method at all.

The fix is two lines: mount the same handler on PUT, and make the client send PUT. I kept PATCH registered as well, so the API stays honest about REST semantics while the deployed path uses a verb the gateway accepts. I wrote the reason into the README, because a future reader will otherwise "clean up" the duplicate route.
Bug three: a whitespace character in an environment variable

Logging in with the correct password returned 500 while a wrong password returned 401. That asymmetry narrowed it to jwt.sign — the code had already found the user. The error was: "expiresIn" should be a number of seconds. The value was 7d. It looked like 7d.

It was not. A zero-width character had come along when the value was pasted into the console. Deleting the variable and letting the code fall back to its default fixed it. Lesson: when a config value fails validation while looking correct, suspect the bytes, not the logic. I now print the JSON-stringified value, not the value.

A related one: environment variables on this platform are injected when an instance starts. Saving them in the console does nothing until you redeploy the code. The health endpoint returns uptime, so "did the restart actually happen" has an objective answer — uptime goes back to zero or it does not.
Bug four: deep links and a sub-path

A static host has no idea that /projects/6ae6d5 is a route. Without a fallback it returns 404 and the reader sees nothing. Copying the built index.html to 404.html fixes it in one line. Then a second, quieter problem: the site is served from /crisfu-capstone/, not from the domain root, so every absolute asset path and the router basename have to agree. Vite's base option handles the assets; the router needs the same value passed as basename. Miss either one and the page loads with a blank screen and a 404 for its own JavaScript.
How I know it works now

Three layers, because "it looked fine" is not evidence. 68 assertions against the API covering auth, ownership (a second account gets 403 on someone else's project), validation, and 404 on malformed ids. A headless-browser pass that drives the real site against the real API: sign in, create a project, confirm it is in the database, delete it, confirm it is gone, post a comment, submit the contact form, watch the inbox counter move. And a manual pass from a second device, on a different network, because that is the only way to catch the things localhost hides.

The honest summary: the application code was the easy part. What made it a finished project was treating the deployment path as part of the design — assuming the gateway will rewrite a header, that a verb might be blocked, that a config value might carry an invisible character, and that a 404 page is a routing feature rather than an error.
What I would do differently

Choose the hosting target before writing the auth layer, not after. I rebuilt the entry point three times — Express listener, then serverless handler, then a second serverless dialect — because each platform wanted a different shape. The adapter is thin, but writing it three times is a week I could have spent on the client.
And set the environment variables on day one. Two of the four bugs above were configuration, not code, and both cost an evening.

posts.title: Why I shipped an entire web app inside one HTML file
posts.excerpt: No build step, no dependencies, no install instructions. A file you double-click is still the fastest way to get someone to actually try your thing.

body.text: The debate simulator is one HTML file. Not a bundle that happens to be inlined — no build step, no node_modules, no CDN. You double-click it and it runs. That decision was not an aesthetic one; it was about who would actually open it.
The friction tax

Every extra step before someone sees your work costs you a large share of your audience. Clone, install, configure an env file, run a dev server — that is four chances to lose a teacher, a classmate, or a recruiter who is looking at your link on a phone.
If the demo needs instructions, it is not a demo yet.
A single file removes all four. It also forces a discipline I did not expect: when everything lives in one place, dead code is impossible to ignore.
What it costs

items: No modules. I used one IIFE and named things carefully.
No framework. State changes are explicit DOM updates, which is fine at this size and painful at twice this size.
No tree shaking. The file is 160 KB, which is smaller than most hero images.

body.text: The line is around 3000 lines. Past that, I would reach for a bundler without hesitating. Below it, the single file wins on nearly every axis that matters for a demo.
The trick that made it work

Data first. I wrote the 100 topics as a plain array before any UI existed, then wrote a checker that verified every sample argument contains at least two of its own keywords. That checker found 348 problems in my own writing.
That is the part people do not see when they open the file. The file is small; the validation behind it is not.

posts.title: Where should a JWT live? localStorage vs. cookies, settled
posts.excerpt: Both options are wrong in the same way, and both are right in a different way. The answer depends on one question: who is allowed to run JavaScript on your page?

body.text: Every tutorial says 'store the token in localStorage' and every security article says 'never store a token in localStorage'. They are both describing real trade-offs, badly.
The actual difference
localStorage is readable by any JavaScript running on your origin. Cookies marked HttpOnly are not. That is the whole security argument, and everything else is consequence.

items: localStorage — one successful XSS and the attacker walks away with a long-lived credential.
HttpOnly cookie — XSS cannot read it, but the browser will attach it to requests you did not intend, so you now need CSRF protection.

body.text: So which one

For a course project where the frontend and API live on different domains, I use localStorage plus a short expiry and a refresh endpoint. It is the option that does not require cookie domain gymnastics across two deploy targets, and the risk profile of a portfolio site is low.
For anything holding real user data, I would use an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Lax cookie with a CSRF token — and accept the extra moving parts.
localStorage is not insecure. It is insecure the moment you have an XSS bug, which is a different sentence.
The one thing I would not do is keep the token in React state only. A refresh then logs the user out, and users read that as a bug, not as security.

posts.title: Scoring a robot's argument: tuning a five-axis rubric
posts.excerpt: The hard part of grading an argument is not detecting keywords. It is refusing to reward confidence.

body.text: The first version of the debate scorer counted keywords. It gave full marks to 'Reading is good, because reading is good, and everyone knows reading is good' — three keyword hits, zero arguments.
Five axes, and why

items: Logic — 'because / so / if / then' structure. Highest weight, because it is the thing being taught.
Relevance — does it touch this topic's keywords, including synonyms.
Length — a weak signal on its own, so it caps early.
Rebuttal — does it engage with the other side, not just restate its own.
Examples — a concrete case earns more than a general claim.

body.text: Slogans are detected separately: a phrase like 'obviously' or 'needless to say' is stripped before scoring, and if nothing substantive is left, the score is zero rather than low.
Negative scores are a feature

Cheating, hitting someone, lying — these are not weak arguments, they are bad ones, and a rubric that treats them as 'a bit off-topic' teaches the wrong lesson. One sentence cost four points in testing, which felt right: recoverable, but memorable.

const pen = detectHarmful(text); // cheating, violence, insults
if (pen.length) return { score: -4 * pen.length, stars: 0, comments: [...] };
The rubric is not fair in any deep sense. But it is consistent, explainable, and every point it awards has a sentence attached — which is more than most automated grading can say.

posts.title: The CSS I keep re-typing in every project
posts.excerpt: Eleven lines that fixed 80% of my layout complaints, and one line I should have written years earlier.

body.text: I have started every project by pasting the same block of CSS. It is not a framework and it will never be one, but it removes the four problems I hit first every single time.
The line I resisted

overflow-x:hidden on body. For years I treated horizontal scroll as a bug to be found. Usually it is a decorative element — a blurred glow, a rotated caption — sitting slightly outside the viewport, and clipping it is the correct fix, not a cover-up.
What is not in the block

items: No reset library. I want the browser defaults for headings and lists to survive.
No spacing scale. I add one when a page actually needs it.
No colour system until the second page exists — the first page always lies about what it needs.

posts.title: What MongoDB actually taught me about schemas
posts.excerpt: Schemaless does not mean no design. It means the design lives in your queries, where it is much harder to see.

body.text: I came to MongoDB from a course that spent six weeks on normalisation, so my first instinct was to split everything into collections and join them back with populate(). Six months later I mostly do the opposite.
Embed what you read together

A blog post and its comments are read together and written separately. But comments per post are small and bounded in a portfolio site, so embedding them means one query serves the detail page — and the 'count the comments' problem disappears.
Model the read path first. The write path is easier to change.
Indexes are the schema you can feel

A marketplace search by faculty and condition was 'slow' until we added a compound index in that order. Same query, same data, ten times faster. In a relational database I would have thought about this at design time; in Mongo it is easy to pretend it does not matter.
listingSchema.index({ faculty: 1, condition: 1, createdAt: -1 });
The honest summary: Mongo let me ship before I understood my data, and then charged interest on that loan.
